title: Difficulty–Diversity Collaborative Filtering for Data-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
claim: Factorizing a binary correctness matrix into model and question embeddings yields difficulty scores and similarity signals for selecting compact, diverse training subsets.
layout: 1 row, left-to-right matrix equation, color-coded heatmap and colorbar at right
description: A single horizontal matrix equation read left to right. On the left is a 4x4 binary correctness matrix. Its rows are LLMs shown by logos (Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral) and its columns are questions Q1–Q4, filled with 1s and 0s. An approximation sign leads to a tall model-embedding matrix with empty cells, multiplied by a short wide question-embedding matrix, also empty. An equals sign leads to a factorized matrix of predicted correctness scores such as 1.0, 0.3 and 0.0. Cells are colored from green (easy) to red (hard), and a vertical green-to-red colorbar is labeled Easy and Hard. An arc over the Q1 and Q4 columns reads 'High similarity → Undiversified'. Plain black text labels sit under each matrix. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmap on the right.
caption: An illustration of our proposed Difficulty–Diversity Collaborative Filtering framework. Given a dataset, a binary correctness matrix from model predictions is factorized into model and question embeddings. Difficulty is defined by factorized scores, while diversity is measured by question similarity. These two criteria jointly guide the selection of compact yet effective training subsets, providing strong learning signals while avoiding redundant, overly similar examples.
abstract: The performance of fine-tuned language models is heavily influenced by the quality and quantity of their fine-tuning data. While scaling laws suggest that larger models benefit from more data during pretraining, the Less-is-More hypothesis highlights that downstream fine-tuning often requires only a small but high-quality dataset to effectively elicit a model’s pretrained knowledge. However, identifying such premium data, particularly in terms of difficulty and diversity, typically relies on human expertise, and existing methods offer limited guidance for automatic selection from large unannotated corpora. This work presents a novel quantitative framework that formalizes the interplay between question difficulty and diversity, and introduces *Difficulty–Diversity Collaborative Filtering* (DDCF): an automated approach that tailors data selection to the unique characteristics of each language model via collaborative filtering. By leveraging a small seed dataset to predict correctness across a large unannotated corpus, our method reduces the annotation cost by $100-200\times$, while maintaining downstream performance comparable to full-corpus fine-tuning.
